chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the white thread from the black thread, so he said: 'The whiteness of the day from the blackness of the night.' He said: 'Bilal used to call the Adhan for the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and Ibn Umm Maktoum (who was blind) used to call the Adhan at night, and Bilal would call the Adhan when dawn emerged. So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'When you hear the voice of Bilal, then stop eating and drinking, for it has become morning.'

key_terms.ابْنُ أُمِّ مَكْتُومٍ: Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, a blind companion who called Adhan at night
key_terms.الْخَيْطِ الْأَبْيَضِ: The white thread (referring to the white light of dawn)
key_terms.الْخَيْطِ الْأَسْوَدِ: The black thread (referring to the blackness of night)
key_terms.بِلَالٌ: Bilal ibn Rabah, the companion known for calling the Adhan

ai.seo_question: When does the time for ending the pre-dawn meal begin during Ramadan fasting?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi elucidates the Quranic metaphor of the 'white and black thread' by identifying them as the visual distinction between night and dawn, a concept central to Shia jurisprudence regarding the precise timing of Fajr. It highlights the historical practice where Bilal’s Adhan served as the definitive legal marker for ending Suhoor, emphasizing that the prohibition begins at the actual appearance of dawn rather than a fixed clock time. This narration underscores the importance of observable natural signs in establishing religious obligations.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father and Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, altogether from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al Halby who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the (distinction of the) white thread from the black thread. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: (It is) the whiteness of the day from the blackness of the night’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Bilal used to call the Azan for the Prophet<sup>saww</sup>, and Ibn Am Maktoum, and he was blind, would call the Azan at night, and Bilal would call the Azan when the dawn emerged. So the Prophet<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘When you hear Bilal, so leave the food and the drink, for it would have become a morning’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from and Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad all from ibn abu ‘Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabiy who has said the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of ‘The white twine from the black twine.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘It is the whiteness of the day out of the blackness of the night.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Bilal and ibn ‘Umm Maktum would say Adhan for the Holy prophet. Ibn ‘Umm Maktum was blind and would say Adhan in the night. Bilal, however, would say Adhan when it was dawn. The Holy prophet said, ‘When you hear the voice of Bilal then stop eating and drinking, because you are in the morning.’”
